nameStory: The romantic name "love-lies-bleeding" comes from the plant's long, drooping flower clusters that cascade downward like crimson tears or drops of blood. The "love" part likely refers to the flower's deep red color, traditionally associated with passion, while the "bleeding" describes how the dense, velvety flower tassels seem to drip from the plant like flowing blood.
description: Love-lies-bleeding is a striking annual flower that looks like it belongs in a Victorian garden drama. This upright plant produces the most remarkable feature: long, rope-like clusters of tiny deep red or crimson flowers that hang down like thick, velvety tassels, sometimes reaching a foot or more in length. The plant itself can grow 3-6 feet tall with broad, oval leaves, creating an eye-catching display that's impossible to miss when in bloom. Originally from South America, it's now grown as an ornamental flower around the world.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Long, drooping, rope-like clusters of tiny deep red flowers that feel soft and velvety to the touch, hanging down like thick tassels or chenille fabric

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual plant growing 3-6 feet tall with sturdy, somewhat thick stems that support the heavy flower clusters

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Broad, oval-shaped leaves arranged alternately along the stem, with a smooth texture and prominent veins

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, shiny black seeds that fall easily from the dried flower clusters and can be collected by running your hand along the spent tassels

habitat: In New England, love-lies-bleeding is primarily found in cultivated gardens, flower beds, and sometimes as an escape near old homesteads or abandoned gardens. It prefers well-drained, fertile soil and full sun locations. You might occasionally spot it growing wild in disturbed areas like vacant lots or roadsides where seeds have dispersed from nearby gardens.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge from seed with characteristic broad, oval leaves. In cultivation, seeds are often started indoors or planted directly in late spring after frost danger passes.
seasonality.summer: The spectacular drooping flower tassels develop and reach their peak display in mid to late summer, creating the plant's most recognizable feature.
seasonality.fall: Flowers begin to fade and dry, turning brown while producing abundant tiny black seeds that scatter easily. Plants die with the first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants are completely gone, leaving only scattered seeds in the soil that may germinate the following spring.

funFact: The seeds of love-lies-bleeding are actually a nutritional powerhouse that was a staple food for the Aztecs and Incas - they're still eaten today and are completely gluten-free, containing more protein than wheat and all the essential amino acids your body needs!
confusionNotes: Love-lies-bleeding is most likely to be confused with other amaranths, but none of the wild species in New England have the distinctive long, drooping flower clusters. Wild amaranths typically have upright, dense flower spikes rather than the cascading tassels. Remember: if it's "bleeding" downward, it's love-lies-bleeding!
contextualKnowledge: This plant is part of the amaranth family, and "amaranth" comes from the Greek word meaning "unfading," referring to how the dried flowers retain their color and form. In South America, where it originates, it's known as "kiwicha" and is still cultivated as an important food crop, making it both a beautiful ornamental and an ancient superfood.
compareHints: Love-lies-bleeding stands out dramatically from its wild amaranth relatives in New England because of its long, pendulous flower clusters - all the others have upright, spike-like flower heads. While redroot amaranth and smooth pigweed have dense, erect flower spikes, love-lies-bleeding's tassels hang down like decorative rope. The cultivated origin also means it's typically much larger and more robust than its weedy cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England amaranths, redroot is distinguished by its reddish taproot and compact, bristly flower clusters.
Unlike the weedy Redroot Amaranth found in gardens and fields, Tidalmarsh Amaranth is strictly a coastal specialist that grows much taller and in dense colonies.

Purple amaranth stands out from its amaranth relatives by its distinctly prostrate, mat-forming growth habit - while redroot amaranth and smooth pigweed grow upright like small bushes, purple amaranth sprawls along the ground.
Among its amaranth relatives, red amaranth stands out for its particularly robust, upright growth and thick, erect flower spikes.
Compared to redroot amaranth, smooth pigweed has less hairy stems and leaves, and its flower spikes tend to be more upright rather than drooping.
Among the New England amaranths, rough-fruit amaranth stands out for its preference for wetter habitats and its distinctively bumpy seeds.
Among New England's amaranths, green amaranth is unique for maintaining its green color throughout the season - most others develop reddish or purplish tones in stems, roots, or flower clusters.
Among New England's amaranths, spiny amaranth is the only one with actual spines - species like redroot amaranth and smooth pigweed may have bristly flowers but lack the sharp spines at leaf bases.
Palmer's Amaranth stands out from its amaranth relatives because it's 'dioecious' - meaning individual plants are either male or female, not both like most other amaranths.
Powell's amaranth differs from redroot amaranth by lacking the red-tinged roots and having less hairy leaves.
Unlike its weedy cousins like Redroot Amaranth that grow tall and upright in disturbed soils, Seabeach Amaranth stays flat against the sand and has much thicker, more succulent leaves and stems.
